title: The Golden Age of British Ice Cream
excerpt: Cornetto to Magnum: How fifteen influential years changed British culture. Words by Ruby Tandoh. Illustration by Sing Yun Lee.
content_html:
Good morning and welcome to Vittles. Today’s essay by Ruby Tandoh is about the most influential decade-and-a-half in British ice cream culture — a fertile period from 1976 to 1991 during which most of the ice creams you’ll find in a British freezer today were invented. This essay is adapted from Ruby’s book All Consuming, which was released in paperback last month. To buy it, please click here.

Today’s article is also part of our online-only series of essays on influence linked to our third print issue, ‘The Influencers’ which officially came out last week. Thanks to everyone who has bought a copy so far! You can order your copy here, and, while you’re there, you may as well throw in a copy of Ruby’s ice cream guide too.

The golden age of British ice cream started with a simple enough gambit: that there had to be a way of packaging the iconic ice cream cone. What if, instead of having to queue up outside a seaside ice cream hut, or a transient ice cream van, you could go into a shop – any shop – and find a cornet waiting for you, pre-made? What if it was fixed so that it was perfect every time – so that a smooth, dense volume of ice cream went all the way down into the cone, so that sauce ran through the ruffles and never fully froze and never dripped? What if you could make it so that it was physically impossible for the ice cream to fall off the cone?

An Italian manufacturer called Spica had already got the formula down in 1959. The success was partly down to the cone Spica designed: a bias-cut, crisp wafer construction that had been sprayed on the inside with a mixture of chocolate and coconut oil, forming a damp-proof barrier between the wafer and the ice cream. But the ice cream was important too. Full-dairy ice cream doesn’t hold up well when you try to pipe it or store it like this. The new ice cream was different. It felt colder on the tongue. It melted quickly but smoothly, with the precision of a racer taking a clean, sharp bend. What you ended up with was a cornet of compactly aerated vegetable-fat emulsion threaded with sauce, serving mainly as a pretext for the chocolate plug.

The ice cream did well in the homeland of gelato, but in Britain, the idea didn’t immediately translate. There’s only so long that wet ice cream can last in a crisp sugar cone before things start to break down, and the turnover of ice cream in a corner shop in Bolton wasn’t like that in a store in Rimini. So, when Wall’s – the biggest name in British ice cream – tried to launch it in the UK in the mid-sixties, it crashed out. It took ten more years of chemical tweaking to hit the impossible sweet spot: an ice cream with the physical qualities of Teflon that could withstand getting knocked around in a freezer cabinet but that also melted in the mouth. Eventually they nailed it, and Wall’s parent company Unilever bought the recipe. In the summer of 1976, the Cornetto entered the British corner shop.

Nearly 7 million Cornettos were sold that summer. You couldn’t have chosen a better time to release an ice cream. It was one of the hottest summers on record, with ice cream season extending long into autumn, and that same year, semi-luxury ice cream chains Baskin-Robbins and Dayvilles both entered the UK market and got people used to the idea that you might pay as much as 25p for an ice cream cone. Walls marketed hard, coming up with a proto-viral campaign - the ‘Just One Cornetto’ song. Within a decade, Cornetto had variants in strawberry, mint, and rum and raisin flavours, and was selling 70 million units a year. It was by far the most popular ice cream Britain had ever produced.

In the world of British ice cream, 1976 was the beginning of an influential fifteen-year purple patch that spawned pretty much every one of the ice creams you find in the freezers today. Go to a shop or browse the menu on the side of an ice cream van. You see the Mini Milks? 1976. Funny Feet – the ancestor of skinless, sculptural ice creams in the shape of Minions and Peppa Pig – debuted in 1980. The Twister, the coiled ice cream and sorbet hybrid? The format was invented in 1982 in Ireland as a strawberry, vanilla and chocolate ice cream, with the flavours it has today – the lime, pineapple and strawberry trifecta – allegedly, incomprehensibly, the result of a schoolgirl’s trip to the Gloucester Wall’s factory in 1987 courtesy of Jim’ll Fix It. Viennetta was invented in 1982. Calippo came to the UK in 1982, although the orange Calippo wasn’t launched until 1988. Feast – a horrible ice cream that seems unkillable in a hard-shelled, cockroach kind of way – was 1983. In 1988, we got Mars ice cream bars. In 1990, Carte d’Or. Bookending the period, was another titan launched in 1990 that surpassed even the Cornetto: the Magnum – the most popular ice cream in the world today.

This sudden leap forward in ice cream culture may seem mysterious, but it is often how things work once food gets to an industrial scale. Change happens quickly, and innovation comes in waves – amplified by economic changes, mergers, acquisitions and low-stakes corporate arms races. In the 1930s it happened with chocolate, with the release of Mars bars, Snickers, Milky Bar, Maltesers, Aero, Ritter Sport, Rolos and KitKats – a chocolate-bar formal repertoire we haven’t meaningfully improved upon almost a century later. Something similar has happened in the last few years: an era of unprecedented creativity in crisp flavourings. The golden age of ice cream was just fifteen years, roughly overlaying the late seventies and eighties, but it saw the biggest explosion of industrial British food culture in the last half century.

When ice cream was popularised in the UK in the late 1800s, it would have been hard to imagine that things would go this far. Italian migrants sold penny lick milk ices on the streets, sellers convening on the canals in the early morning to buy blocks of ice, then dispersing across the city. Milk was frozen with sugar and, maybe, egg; serving glasses were wiped out with an old rag and then refilled to order. Over time, the ice creams became more complex; during the thirties, the catering and cafe empire Lyons made ice cream cakes – campy things like Trocadero Wonder Gateau and Glace Pompadour, with ice cream moulded like a ball-gown skirt.

By the start of the World War 2, there were armadas of men on tricycles selling ice creams under the branding of Wall’s – a sausage manufacturer that had realised, astutely enough, that people weren’t really buying pork pies in summertime and so it probably needed a second income stream – which had been acquired by the progenitor of Unilever in 1922. Ice cream, however, was extraneous to the war effort and restrictions were put on how much dairy and sugar the industry could use. By the fifties, ice cream was more basic than ever; most Lyons ice cream – eventually brought under the banner of Lyons Maid – was rigorously functional: bricks, bricklets, cups, poles and rectangular choc ices.

With the end of rationing in 1954, the final wartime restrictions on food were lifted and spending power increased. During the war, the fleets of ice cream tricycles had been sold and scrapped, but they were succeeded by ice cream vans and convenience stores. Wall’s, which had once sold 90% of its ice cream on the road, now sold 90% from the capacious freezer cabinets of brick-and-mortar shops, from whose owners they could demand exclusivity. All of a sudden, and pretty much out of nothing, there was an opportunity to do something new.

The first technologically cutting-edge ice creams were basic by today’s standards. Take the Lyons Maid Mivvi, a fruit split with a strawberry or orange ice shell around vanilla ice cream on a stick that debuted in 1959. It was simple, but undergirded by some of the most complex technologies of the time. Fruit-flavoured syrup was pumped from plastic arteries into rows of moulds, a two-handed manoeuvre in which the moulds advanced in time with the pulse. Mechanical arms swung the moulds through a cryogenically cold brine bath, a motion just smooth enough to be legible to the human eye, during which a crust of fruit ice a few millimetres thick froze to the contours of the metal. After this, the moulds were inverted with the snap of a flamenco dancer’s wrist, tipping the unfrozen centres into a vat. Then, ice cream was piped into the empty shells through exacting metal mouths and wooden lolly sticks were shot from muzzles lining the sides of the conveyor. A machine like this could make tens of thousands of strawberry splits every hour. After it launched, over a third of the Lyons Maid ice cream sold came on a stick.

Technological changes in the sixties and seventies led to ice creams, predominantly geared towards children, that would’ve been unimaginable even a decade earlier. We got Haunted House ice lollies, which had blue ghosts printed into white milk ice. A new blood-red Dracula-inspired lolly had the craftsman’s line of a medieval gargoyle. As you licked a Magic Monster lolly, the face of Frankenstein’s monster appeared through the ice. Fab – an underskirt of strawberry ice, a wraparound of vanilla ice cream and an outer layer of sprinkle- beaded chocolate – was inspired by Lady Penelope’s FAB1 Rolls-Royce from Thunderbirds.

This particular thread of ice cream was beginning to wear out by the mid-seventies. The products being introduced were popular enough, but they were cheap and mainly bought by kids. Slowly, more people got home freezers, which opened space for bigger, take-home tubs of ice cream and supermarket multipacks of their own-brand lollies. Companies like Unilever had to come up with something bigger and better if they wanted to avoid going the way of Lyons Maid, which is to say, sliding into total irrelevance. When Walls struck gold with the Cornetto in 1976, it was the first of many answers to one simple question that would guide the company’s strategy for the next five decades: ‘How do you sell ice cream to grown-ups?’

In the years after 1976, Walls tried to improve and iterate on the Cornetto without much success. The man who finally managed to do it was Kevin Hillman, a product developer who started at Unilever on a scholarship in 1958 and didn’t leave until his retirement in 2001. For most of that time, he worked in ice cream, doing the imaginative acrobatics that you’d expect from Willy Wonka, but with granular attention to detail in the matter of things like emulsification, viscosity and the complex chemistry of milk. He was once head of product development for Unilever’s take-home ice cream – that is, the big tubs and desserts that you don’t eat on the go (in the ice cream world, all products are divided into take-home or impulse, which refers to Cornettos or anything on a stick).

By 1980, Hillman was a product development manager at the new Wall’s production plant in Gloucester. One day, when looking through a Good Housekeeping cookbook that he’d bought his wife, he saw a recipe for millefeuille: three sheets of puff pastry, each one with around 729 layers of buttery carbs and air, mortared with two layers of thick vanilla custard or cream. Hillman began to wonder what an ice cream millefeuille would look like. You could extrude drifts of ice cream, but instead of sandwiching them with pastry – which would soften and warp – you could interpolate them with the thinnest leaves of chocolate, he thought. Until the late seventies, take-home ice cream was a support act to impulse, but Hillman’s team had begun to experiment with ice creams that were good enough to work a crowd. Wall’s had already tried out Arctic roll, wrapping a log of vanilla ice cream in a jam-slicked sleeve of sponge cake, and there were also experiments in strawberry- and chocolate-flavoured log desserts, the foundations of a sundae compacted into a 600ml rectangular ice cream block.

The earliest prototypes of Hillman’s idea were basic – just the size of a Vesta matchbox, with rigid layers that tasted great but visually fell flat. But Wall’s discovered that if you squeezed a length of steel pipe in a vice until it had an aperture of just a few millimetres, you could extrude very broad, thin sheets of ice cream in an unbroken stream; in time, they also realised that if you increased the output speed, the ice cream would begin to pile up in collapsing sine waves. The engineers worked on adapting the machinery so that the process of plastic extrusion could be used to make something like edible art. In between each of the dozen ice cream layers, they sprayed atomically thin, stracciatella-style layers of chocolate, using an Elizabethan ruff as a visual reference. The result was a dessert the same size as the Motorola 8000X, an early, brick-like mobile phone that debuted that same year. When the team at Wall’s drafted the patent, they described ‘Composite confection products [that] comprise a multiplicity of superimposed extruded thin layers of extrudable e.g. aerated frozen confection, optionally separated by interleaved very thin second confection layers such as couverture thin enough to be at least partly discontinuous.’ But on the streets, they called it Viennetta.

If you’re talking to anyone about ice cream’s greatest generation, Hillman’s name will inevitably come up for the Viennetta alone. But if you press him too hard about it, he gets shy. The Viennetta origin story is the kind of thing that is constantly brought up and broken down and misremembered; we like to hear fairy tales about these kinds of foods – the foods that are everywhere but that none of us knows how to make – but they are painstakingly engineered by teams at costs running into millions to game our dopamine systems into buying more. Hillman knows this better than anyone, which is why, when I interviewed him last year and asked about the lightbulb moment, he politely referred me to a corporate history book (Renewing Unilever: Transformation and Tradition) and left it at that.

But when I got him on to the real lineage of this ice cream – the myriad corporate, commercial, industrial and trans-European forces that led to the invention of Viennetta – he jumped right in. The spray guns for those ultra-thin layers of chocolate couverture were a trick they took from Cornettos: ‘Exactly the same technology,’ he noted, ‘is used to spray chocolate as is used to spray paint on cars.’ The ice cream, too, was the same as that used in Cornettos – that bright white, sculptable, continental-style ice cream made using vegetable fat, which gives the ice cream its plastic properties, arguably at the expense of taste. Unilever came from the merger of a Dutch margarine company and a British soap business, which means that it was set up nicely for the rise of highly processed vegetable-fat-based ice creams (Dutch colonial links to Indonesia made coconut oil a sure bet.) Then there was the packaging, which was borrowed from Unilever’s German ice cream brand, Langnese.

‘We had very close links. We could pick up the phone and get anything from [other Unilever factories in] Europe,’ Hillman told me. This is how Britain came to host the most productive decade in ice cream, globally, ever: it didn’t do it alone. Unilever had been slowly acquiring ice cream businesses from across the continent for decades. That particular white ice cream is a rethink of an Italian ice cream, perfected under Unilever’s Belgian business, marketed in the UK. Sometimes the impetus for creativity is romance, but most of the time it’s something more prosaic – a Medici, or a Unilever. The story of ice cream is really one of corporate tactics and injections of cash, of the movements of huge companies to create, and then aggressively enforce, a new agenda.

After Viennetta blew up, Unilever tried to squeeze a few more ice creams from that basic idea. They developed things like Romantica, Carissima, Sonata and Cassata Denice – all Italianate ice cream gateaux with the kinds of names a person would use to catfish on a sugar daddy site. In 1985, the company started ‘Project Renaissance’, exploring the hypothetical that ice cream could be, instead of a kids’ thing, ‘a secret affair – a lover to be “used”’. Look through the patent records and you’ll find dozens of patents for new ice cream ideas. There’s an ice cream inside a brandysnap-style tuile, capped with waxy chocolate at the ends. There’s another for a lolly made using tiny pellets of fruit ice, poured into a mould, and then frozen together with a contrasting-flavour ice cement. Everyone was doing it. Over at Lyons Maid, they rebranded their choc ice as Figaro and developed the Caprice – a chocolate bar with malt ice cream and caramel that now persists only in lore. Nutcracker, a vanilla ice cream bar with toffee sauce and peanuts, joined Caprice in what was marketed at the time as an ‘adult connoisseur range’.

The trouble with marketing ice cream to adults is that novelty isn’t enough. You need things to actually taste great, or at least to taste as luxe as they look. In the eighties, the principles of ice cream began to change, with a new focus on ingredient quality. Lyons Maid introduced a Gold Seal range, then Crème de la Crème – seemingly arbitrary gradations of luxuriousness. In France, Carte d’Or found a path from wholesale into the retail market. Pillsbury bought and popularised the pseudo-Scandinavian Häagen-Dazs. Ben & Jerry’s, which started as a shop in a Vermont garage, opened its first factory in 1985, sold on the strength of its countercultural credentials and natural ingredients. ‘Wanted!’ ran one Lyons Maid advert. ‘Real chocolate, real goodness, real fruit and double cream.’

Around this time, European subsidiaries of Unilever were developing a simple ice cream – vanilla, enrobed in chocolate, on a stick. It was the polar opposite of Cornetto and Viennetta, despite working towards the same grown-up principles. It had real vanilla ice cream, enriched not with coconut oil but with butterfat. Whereas most of the chocolate that Unilever had been using was imitation – cheap and adaptable, setting either to a waxy cap or the thinnest layer of craquelure – for this ice cream it developed a better kind of chocolate, one that could be deep-frozen, and that snapped loudly into big, angular shards, but still melted in the mouth. They experimented with the recipe, took it back to basics, and gave the lolly a smooth, cursive silhouette. The industry, which for much of the eighties had evolved in the same implausible way as a deep-sea fish, returned to simple forms. The Magnum debuted in Germany in 1989, and hit the UK the year after.

At the end of the day, a Magnum is a choc ice. But what a choc ice! ‘Magnumize your free time’, an ad would say, and show a woman lock the kids outside, so she can go hard on her Magnum in peace. ‘Magnumize your life’: at the office, she has unplugged the landline master socket. (It’s hard to capture just how horny the Magnum was.) If Wall’s started selling ice cream to get through the fallow summer months, then Unilever smashed the final frontier by finding a way to market ice cream all year round – any time, any place. It wasn’t about the sun or refreshment any more, but just an adult’s right to a moment of pleasure. In 1990, for their first big stunt, and the last truly exciting day in British ice cream, Magnums were handed out to thousands of commuters in three major London stations, in rush hour, in November. Within a couple of years, it was the best-selling ice cream in the world, and remains so today.

‘Of all the fast foods on sale in Britain,’ the food writer Jane Grigson wrote in the Observer at the start of 1990, ‘I would say that vanilla ice cream represents the most catastrophic fall from original virtue.’ But Grigson died just a couple of months later and so I have to wonder if she ever got the chance to try a Magnum?

The ice creams that came out of the golden age are as much a part of British food culture as cheddar cheese is. In fact, there are a lot of parallels between the two. Like cheese, ice cream is a dairy product that was given new vitality in the eighties. In the case of cheese, it was by looking back to traditional methods of cheesemaking. In the case of the ice cream, it was innovation, rather than revival, and it happened on the biggest imaginable scale. But unlike the cheese side of the dairy industry, which has continued to thrive, ice cream has stagnated.

It’s not like people haven’t tried. In the early nineties, Kevin Hillman was fine-tuning the recipe for a new fruit version of Romantica – a Viennetta-inspired gateau constructed with stacked rosettes of vanilla and strawberry ice cream and sprinkled with beads of fruit ice. He found that if you used a kind of rudimentary shower head, you could spray globular drops of fruit syrup into a bath of liquid nitrogen, where they instantly froze into hailstones. Romantica never took off, but the idea was eventually recycled as Calippo – and then Solero – Shots: tiny pellets of fruit ice that you tipped back like the crumbs at the end of a bag of crisps. This was, for ice cream aficionados, a moment of hope, but these were discontinued within a few years and nothing good has really happened since.

Today, if you look in that corner-shop freezer cabinet, there will be a Cornetto, a malformed Twister, and then a clade of Magnums: classic, double caramel, white chocolate, almond, mint. The novelties: Starchaser Chocolate Caramel & Popcorn; Gold Caramel Billionaire; Sunlover White Chocolate. Even in the same flavours, Magnums keep on finding culinary synonyms, from vegan Magnums to Magnum ice cream tubs (the chocolate shell turned into an upper crust), mini Magnums and Magnum bites. Everything else, from the chocolate ice cream bars launched by Mars, to the Solero, is a version of a Magnum. It never ends. Last year, Unilever demerged its entire ice cream portfolio, including all the ice creams of the Wall’s Golden Age, and remerged them into a new entity: The Magnum Ice Cream Company. The Magnum has ended up more famous than the company that birthed it.

Last year I went to a food industry expo at London’s ExCel Centre to see if the industry was turning out ice creams that I didn’t yet know about, but should. I hoped to see the prototypes of a new generation of ice creams, the technological and imaginative vanguard. What I saw was a vegan non-Cornetto brand at an unmanned stall. There was a Romanian manufacturer of ice creams modelled after Magnums, making a push for relevance after Unilever entered the Romanian market with the real thing. There were health-food anti-Soleros made from plant juice, fibre and pulp. A Slovenian brand had a product poster that could have been photocopied and transliterated from a Wall’s decal from 1989: Everest was a facsimile of a Magnum, Turbo was a Magic-Ice brand Twister, Free was a Maxibon. The only thing that really spoke to the idiosyncrasies of Slovenian taste was Adore – a mini imitation-Viennetta on a stick. I told Kevin Hillman about it, and he started asking questions that I couldn’t answer about exactly how many layers this thing had.

Near the exit of the expo, there was a stall from Jude’s, an upscale British brand in the same vein as Häagen-Dazs. Maybe it’s a sign of how much things have changed that now British ice cream, like cheese, can sell itself on how British it is. They were handing out samples. Clotted cream was doing well. Chocolate, always. The salesperson told me they were doing something different from the multinationals. They tried to give me a sample of ‘blue vanilla’ ice cream coloured with spirulina.

Behind, in the freezer cabinet, there were legally daring Jude’s not-Rockets and not-Mini Milks, indistinguishable at a glance from the real thing. The Jude’s version of a Twister was called a Fruit Twist: the same maypole but vegan, smaller, lower sugar. I want to say it’s all outdated, but nothing resonates with the current moment quite like constantly reliving, without resolution or growth, the limited victories of the fifteen years that transformed British ice cream culture. Jude’s biggest line was a range of ice cream sticks, not Magnums, but not not Magnums. They were rounded, slightly fatter at the bottom, with dairy ice cream in a thick chocolate shell. Belgian chocolate, salted caramel, peanut butter – the same as always and, maybe, as good as we’ll ever get.

After this, the moulds were inverted with the snap of a flamenco dancer’s wrist, tipping the unfrozen centres into a vat. Then, ice cream was piped into the empty shells through exacting metal mouths and wooden lolly sticks were shot from muzzles lining the sides of the conveyor. A machine like this could make tens of thousands of strawberry splits every hour. After it launched, over a third of the Lyons Maid ice cream sold came on a stick.Technological changes in the sixties and seventies led to ice creams, predominantly geared towards children, that would’ve been unimaginable even a decade earlier. We got Haunted House ice lollies, which had blue ghosts printed into white milk ice. A new blood-red Dracula-inspired lolly had the craftsman’s line of a medieval gargoyle. As you licked a Magic Monster lolly, the face of Frankenstein’s monster appeared through the ice. Fab – an underskirt of strawberry ice, a wraparound of vanilla ice cream and an outer layer of sprinkle- beaded chocolate – was inspired by Lady Penelope’s FAB1 Rolls-Royce from Thunderbirds.This particular thread of ice cream was beginning to wear out by the mid-seventies. The products being introduced were popular enough, but they were cheap and mainly bought by kids. Slowly, more people got home freezers, which opened space for bigger, take-home tubs of ice cream and supermarket multipacks of their own-brand lollies. Companies like Unilever had to come up with something bigger and better if they wanted to avoid going the way of Lyons Maid, which is to say, sliding into total irrelevance. When Walls struck gold with the Cornetto in 1976, it was the first of many answers to one simple question that would guide the company’s strategy for the next five decades: ‘How do you sell ice cream to grown-ups?’A Walls freezer advert in 1976, the year the Cornetto debutedIn the years after 1976, Walls tried to improve and iterate on the Cornetto without much success. The man who finally managed to do it was Kevin Hillman, a product developer who started at Unilever on a scholarship in 1958 and didn’t leave until his retirement in 2001. For most of that time, he worked in ice cream, doing the imaginative acrobatics that you’d expect from Willy Wonka, but with granular attention to detail in the matter of things like emulsification, viscosity and the complex chemistry of milk. He was once head of product development for Unilever’s take-home ice cream – that is, the big tubs and desserts that you don’t eat on the go (in the ice cream world, all products are divided into take-home or impulse, which refers to Cornettos or anything on a stick).By 1980, Hillman was a product development manager at the new Wall’s production plant in Gloucester. One day, when looking through a Good Housekeeping cookbook that he’d bought his wife, he saw a recipe for millefeuille: three sheets of puff pastry, each one with around 729 layers of buttery carbs and air, mortared with two layers of thick vanilla custard or cream. Hillman began to wonder what an ice cream millefeuille would look like. You could extrude drifts of ice cream, but instead of sandwiching them with pastry – which would soften and warp – you could interpolate them with the thinnest leaves of chocolate, he thought. Until the late seventies, take-home ice cream was a support act to impulse, but Hillman’s team had begun to experiment with ice creams that were good enough to work a crowd. Wall’s had already tried out Arctic roll, wrapping a log of vanilla ice cream in a jam-slicked sleeve of sponge cake, and there were also experiments in strawberry- and chocolate-flavoured log desserts, the foundations of a sundae compacted into a 600ml rectangular ice cream block.The earliest prototypes of Hillman’s idea were basic – just the size of a Vesta matchbox, with rigid layers that tasted great but visually fell flat. But Wall’s discovered that if you squeezed a length of steel pipe in a vice until it had an aperture of just a few millimetres, you could extrude very broad, thin sheets of ice cream in an unbroken stream; in time, they also realised that if you increased the output speed, the ice cream would begin to pile up in collapsing sine waves. The engineers worked on adapting the machinery so that the process of plastic extrusion could be used to make something like edible art. In between each of the dozen ice cream layers, they sprayed atomically thin, stracciatella-style layers of chocolate, using an Elizabethan ruff as a visual reference. The result was a dessert the same size as the Motorola 8000X, an early, brick-like mobile phone that debuted that same year. When the team at Wall’s drafted the patent, they described ‘Composite confection products [that] comprise a multiplicity of superimposed extruded thin layers of extrudable e.g. aerated frozen confection, optionally separated by interleaved very thin second confection layers such as couverture thin enough to be at least partly discontinuous.’ But on the streets, they called it Viennetta.The patent for ViennettaIf you’re talking to anyone about ice cream’s greatest generation, Hillman’s name will inevitably come up for the Viennetta alone. But if you press him too hard about it, he gets shy. The Viennetta origin story is the kind of thing that is constantly brought up and broken down and misremembered; we like to hear fairy tales about these kinds of foods – the foods that are everywhere but that none of us knows how to make – but they are painstakingly engineered by teams at costs running into millions to game our dopamine systems into buying more. Hillman knows this better than anyone, which is why, when I interviewed him last year and asked about the lightbulb moment, he politely referred me to a corporate history book (Renewing Unilever: Transformation and Tradition) and left it at that.But when I got him on to the real lineage of this ice cream – the myriad corporate, commercial, industrial and trans-European forces that led to the invention of Viennetta – he jumped right in. The spray guns for those ultra-thin layers of chocolate couverture were a trick they took from Cornettos: ‘Exactly the same technology,’ he noted, ‘is used to spray chocolate as is used to spray paint on cars.’ The ice cream, too, was the same as that used in Cornettos – that bright white, sculptable, continental-style ice cream made using vegetable fat, which gives the ice cream its plastic properties, arguably at the expense of taste. Unilever came from the merger of a Dutch margarine company and a British soap business, which means that it was set up nicely for the rise of highly processed vegetable-fat-based ice creams (Dutch colonial links to Indonesia made coconut oil a sure bet.) Then there was the packaging, which was borrowed from Unilever’s German ice cream brand, Langnese.‘We had very close links. We could pick up the phone and get anything from [other Unilever factories in] Europe,’ Hillman told me. This is how Britain came to host the most productive decade in ice cream, globally, ever: it didn’t do it alone. Unilever had been slowly acquiring ice cream businesses from across the continent for decades. That particular white ice cream is a rethink of an Italian ice cream, perfected under Unilever’s Belgian business, marketed in the UK. Sometimes the impetus for creativity is romance, but most of the time it’s something more prosaic – a Medici, or a Unilever. The story of ice cream is really one of corporate tactics and injections of cash, of the movements of huge companies to create, and then aggressively enforce, a new agenda.Romantica enters the marketAfter Viennetta blew up, Unilever tried to squeeze a few more ice creams from that basic idea. They developed things like Romantica, Carissima, Sonata and Cassata Denice – all Italianate ice cream gateaux with the kinds of names a person would use to catfish on a sugar daddy site. In 1985, the company started ‘Project Renaissance’, exploring the hypothetical that ice cream could be, instead of a kids’ thing, ‘a secret affair – a lover to be “used”’. Look through the patent records and you’ll find dozens of patents for new ice cream ideas. There’s an ice cream inside a brandysnap-style tuile, capped with waxy chocolate at the ends. There’s another for a lolly made using tiny pellets of fruit ice, poured into a mould, and then frozen together with a contrasting-flavour ice cement. Everyone was doing it. Over at Lyons Maid, they rebranded their choc ice as Figaro and developed the Caprice – a chocolate bar with malt ice cream and caramel that now persists only in lore. Nutcracker, a vanilla ice cream bar with toffee sauce and peanuts, joined Caprice in what was marketed at the time as an ‘adult connoisseur range’.The trouble with marketing ice cream to adults is that novelty isn’t enough. You need things to actually taste great, or at least to taste as luxe as they look. In the eighties, the principles of ice cream began to change, with a new focus on ingredient quality. Lyons Maid introduced a Gold Seal range, then Crème de la Crème – seemingly arbitrary gradations of luxuriousness. In France, Carte d’Or found a path from wholesale into the retail market. Pillsbury bought and popularised the pseudo-Scandinavian Häagen-Dazs. Ben & Jerry’s, which started as a shop in a Vermont garage, opened its first factory in 1985, sold on the strength of its countercultural credentials and natural ingredients. ‘Wanted!’ ran one Lyons Maid advert. ‘Real chocolate, real goodness, real fruit and double cream.’Around this time, European subsidiaries of Unilever were developing a simple ice cream – vanilla, enrobed in chocolate, on a stick. It was the polar opposite of Cornetto and Viennetta, despite working towards the same grown-up principles. It had real vanilla ice cream, enriched not with coconut oil but with butterfat. Whereas most of the chocolate that Unilever had been using was imitation – cheap and adaptable, setting either to a waxy cap or the thinnest layer of craquelure – for this ice cream it developed a better kind of chocolate, one that could be deep-frozen, and that snapped loudly into big, angular shards, but still melted in the mouth. They experimented with the recipe, took it back to basics, and gave the lolly a smooth, cursive silhouette. The industry, which for much of the eighties had evolved in the same implausible way as a deep-sea fish, returned to simple forms. The Magnum debuted in Germany in 1989, and hit the UK the year after.At the end of the day, a Magnum is a choc ice. But what a choc ice! ‘Magnumize your free time’, an ad would say, and show a woman lock the kids outside, so she can go hard on her Magnum in peace. ‘Magnumize your life’: at the office, she has unplugged the landline master socket. (It’s hard to capture just how horny the Magnum was.) If Wall’s started selling ice cream to get through the fallow summer months, then Unilever smashed the final frontier by finding a way to market ice cream all year round – any time, any place. It wasn’t about the sun or refreshment any more, but just an adult’s right to a moment of pleasure. In 1990, for their first big stunt, and the last truly exciting day in British ice cream, Magnums were handed out to thousands of commuters in three major London stations, in rush hour, in November. Within a couple of years, it was the best-selling ice cream in the world, and remains so today.‘Of all the fast foods on sale in Britain,’ the food writer Jane Grigson wrote in the Observer at the start of 1990, ‘I would say that vanilla ice cream represents the most catastrophic fall from original virtue.’ But Grigson died just a couple of months later and so I have to wonder if she ever got the chance to try a Magnum?The ice creams that came out of the golden age are as much a part of British food culture as cheddar cheese is. In fact, there are a lot of parallels between the two. Like cheese, ice cream is a dairy product that was given new vitality in the eighties. In the case of cheese, it was by looking back to traditional methods of cheesemaking. In the case of the ice cream, it was innovation, rather than revival, and it happened on the biggest imaginable scale. But unlike the cheese side of the dairy industry, which has continued to thrive, ice cream has stagnated.The last true innovation in ice cream formIt’s not like people haven’t tried. In the early nineties, Kevin Hillman was fine-tuning the recipe for a new fruit version of Romantica – a Viennetta-inspired gateau constructed with stacked rosettes of vanilla and strawberry ice cream and sprinkled with beads of fruit ice. He found that if you used a kind of rudimentary shower head, you could spray globular drops of fruit syrup into a bath of liquid nitrogen, where they instantly froze into hailstones. Romantica never took off, but the idea was eventually recycled as Calippo – and then Solero – Shots: tiny pellets of fruit ice that you tipped back like the crumbs at the end of a bag of crisps. This was, for ice cream aficionados, a moment of hope, but these were discontinued within a few years and nothing good has really happened since.Today, if you look in that corner-shop freezer cabinet, there will be a Cornetto, a malformed Twister, and then a clade of Magnums: classic, double caramel, white chocolate, almond, mint. The novelties: Starchaser Chocolate Caramel & Popcorn; Gold Caramel Billionaire; Sunlover White Chocolate. Even in the same flavours, Magnums keep on finding culinary synonyms, from vegan Magnums to Magnum ice cream tubs (the chocolate shell turned into an upper crust), mini Magnums and Magnum bites. Everything else, from the chocolate ice cream bars launched by Mars, to the Solero, is a version of a Magnum. It never ends. Last year, Unilever demerged its entire ice cream portfolio, including all the ice creams of the Wall’s Golden Age, and remerged them into a new entity: The Magnum Ice Cream Company. The Magnum has ended up more famous than the company that birthed it.Last year I went to a food industry expo at London’s ExCel Centre to see if the industry was turning out ice creams that I didn’t yet know about, but should. I hoped to see the prototypes of a new generation of ice creams, the technological and imaginative vanguard. What I saw was a vegan non-Cornetto brand at an unmanned stall. There was a Romanian manufacturer of ice creams modelled after Magnums, making a push for relevance after Unilever entered the Romanian market with the real thing. There were health-food anti-Soleros made from plant juice, fibre and pulp. A Slovenian brand had a product poster that could have been photocopied and transliterated from a Wall’s decal from 1989: Everest was a facsimile of a Magnum, Turbo was a Magic-Ice brand Twister, Free was a Maxibon. The only thing that really spoke to the idiosyncrasies of Slovenian taste was Adore – a mini imitation-Viennetta on a stick. I told Kevin Hillman about it, and he started asking questions that I couldn’t answer about exactly how many layers this thing had.Near the exit of the expo, there was a stall from Jude’s, an upscale British brand in the same vein as Häagen-Dazs. Maybe it’s a sign of how much things have changed that now British ice cream, like cheese, can sell itself on how British it is. They were handing out samples. Clotted cream was doing well. Chocolate, always. The salesperson told me they were doing something different from the multinationals. They tried to give me a sample of ‘blue vanilla’ ice cream coloured with spirulina.Behind, in the freezer cabinet, there were legally daring Jude’s not-Rockets and not-Mini Milks, indistinguishable at a glance from the real thing. The Jude’s version of a Twister was called a Fruit Twist: the same maypole but vegan, smaller, lower sugar. I want to say it’s all outdated, but nothing resonates with the current moment quite like constantly reliving, without resolution or growth, the limited victories of the fifteen years that transformed British ice cream culture. Jude’s biggest line was a range of ice cream sticks, not Magnums, but not not Magnums. They were rounded, slightly fatter at the bottom, with dairy ice cream in a thick chocolate shell. Belgian chocolate, salted caramel, peanut butter – the same as always and, maybe, as good as we’ll ever get.ShareLeave a commentRuby Tandoh is a food and culture writer who has written about food, art, architecture and culture for Vittles, The New Yorker, The Baffler, Eater, Art Review, RA Magazine, Tate etc., The Guardian and more. blocks.html_en: The golden age of British ice cream started with a simple enough gambit: that there had to be a way of packaging the iconic ice cream cone. What if, instead of having to queue up outside a seaside ice cream hut, or a transient ice cream van, you could go into a shop – any shop – and find a cornet waiting for you, pre-made? What if it was fixed so that it was perfect every time – so that a smooth, dense volume of ice cream went all the way down into the cone, so that sauce ran through the ruffles and never fully froze and never dripped? What if you could make it so that it was physically impossible for the ice cream to fall off the cone?

blocks.html_en: An Italian manufacturer called Spica had already got the formula down in 1959. The success was partly down to the cone Spica designed: a bias-cut, crisp wafer construction that had been sprayed on the inside with a mixture of chocolate and coconut oil, forming a damp-proof barrier between the wafer and the ice cream. But the ice cream was important too. Full-dairy ice cream doesn’t hold up well when you try to pipe it or store it like this. The new ice cream was different. It felt colder on the tongue. It melted quickly but smoothly, with the precision of a racer taking a clean, sharp bend. What you ended up with was a cornet of compactly aerated vegetable-fat emulsion threaded with sauce, serving mainly as a pretext for the chocolate plug.

blocks.html_en: The ice cream did well in the homeland of gelato, but in Britain, the idea didn’t immediately translate. There’s only so long that wet ice cream can last in a crisp sugar cone before things start to break down, and the turnover of ice cream in a corner shop in Bolton wasn’t like that in a store in Rimini. So, when Wall’s – the biggest name in British ice cream – tried to launch it in the UK in the mid-sixties, it crashed out. It took ten more years of chemical tweaking to hit the impossible sweet spot: an ice cream with the physical qualities of Teflon that could withstand getting knocked around in a freezer cabinet but that also melted in the mouth. Eventually they nailed it, and Wall’s parent company Unilever bought the recipe. In the summer of 1976, the Cornetto entered the British corner shop.

blocks.html_en: Nearly 7 million Cornettos were sold that summer. You couldn’t have chosen a better time to release an ice cream. It was one of the hottest summers on record, with ice cream season extending long into autumn, and that same year, semi-luxury ice cream chains Baskin-Robbins and Dayvilles both entered the UK market and got people used to the idea that you might pay as much as 25p for an ice cream cone. Walls marketed hard, coming up with a proto-viral campaign - the ‘Just One Cornetto’ song. Within a decade, Cornetto had variants in strawberry, mint, and rum and raisin flavours, and was selling 70 million units a year. It was by far the most popular ice cream Britain had ever produced.

blocks.html_en: In the world of British ice cream, 1976 was the beginning of an influential fifteen-year purple patch that spawned pretty much every one of the ice creams you find in the freezers today. Go to a shop or browse the menu on the side of an ice cream van. You see the Mini Milks? 1976. Funny Feet – the ancestor of skinless, sculptural ice creams in the shape of Minions and Peppa Pig – debuted in 1980. The Twister, the coiled ice cream and sorbet hybrid? The format was invented in 1982 in Ireland as a strawberry, vanilla and chocolate ice cream, with the flavours it has today – the lime, pineapple and strawberry trifecta – allegedly, incomprehensibly, the result of a schoolgirl’s trip to the Gloucester Wall’s factory in 1987 courtesy of Jim’ll Fix It. Viennetta was invented in 1982. Calippo came to the UK in 1982, although the orange Calippo wasn’t launched until 1988. Feast – a horrible ice cream that seems unkillable in a hard-shelled, cockroach kind of way – was 1983. In 1988, we got Mars ice cream bars. In 1990, Carte d’Or. Bookending the period, was another titan launched in 1990 that surpassed even the Cornetto: the Magnum – the most popular ice cream in the world today.

blocks.html_en: This sudden leap forward in ice cream culture may seem mysterious, but it is often how things work once food gets to an industrial scale. Change happens quickly, and innovation comes in waves – amplified by economic changes, mergers, acquisitions and low-stakes corporate arms races. In the 1930s it happened with chocolate, with the release of Mars bars, Snickers, Milky Bar, Maltesers, Aero, Ritter Sport, Rolos and KitKats – a chocolate-bar formal repertoire we haven’t meaningfully improved upon almost a century later. Something similar has happened in the last few years: an era of unprecedented creativity in crisp flavourings. The golden age of ice cream was just fifteen years, roughly overlaying the late seventies and eighties, but it saw the biggest explosion of industrial British food culture in the last half century.

blocks.html_en: When ice cream was popularised in the UK in the late 1800s, it would have been hard to imagine that things would go this far. Italian migrants sold penny lick milk ices on the streets, sellers convening on the canals in the early morning to buy blocks of ice, then dispersing across the city. Milk was frozen with sugar and, maybe, egg; serving glasses were wiped out with an old rag and then refilled to order. Over time, the ice creams became more complex; during the thirties, the catering and cafe empire Lyons made ice cream cakes – campy things like Trocadero Wonder Gateau and Glace Pompadour, with ice cream moulded like a ball-gown skirt.

blocks.html_en: By the start of the World War 2, there were armadas of men on tricycles selling ice creams under the branding of Wall’s – a sausage manufacturer that had realised, astutely enough, that people weren’t really buying pork pies in summertime and so it probably needed a second income stream – which had been acquired by the progenitor of Unilever in 1922. Ice cream, however, was extraneous to the war effort and restrictions were put on how much dairy and sugar the industry could use. By the fifties, ice cream was more basic than ever; most Lyons ice cream – eventually brought under the banner of Lyons Maid – was rigorously functional: bricks, bricklets, cups, poles and rectangular choc ices.

blocks.html_en: With the end of rationing in 1954, the final wartime restrictions on food were lifted and spending power increased. blocks.html_en: The first technologically cutting-edge ice creams were basic by today’s standards. Take the Lyons Maid Mivvi, a fruit split with a strawberry or orange ice shell around vanilla ice cream on a stick that debuted in 1959. It was simple, but undergirded by some of the most complex technologies of the time. Fruit-flavoured syrup was pumped from plastic arteries into rows of moulds, a two-handed manoeuvre in which the moulds advanced in time with the pulse. Mechanical arms swung the moulds through a cryogenically cold brine bath, a motion just smooth enough to be legible to the human eye, during which a crust of fruit ice a few millimetres thick froze to the contours of the metal. After this, the moulds were inverted with the snap of a flamenco dancer’s wrist, tipping the unfrozen centres into a vat. Then, ice cream was piped into the empty shells through exacting metal mouths and wooden lolly sticks were shot from muzzles lining the sides of the conveyor. A machine like this could make tens of thousands of strawberry splits every hour. After it launched, over a third of the Lyons Maid ice cream sold came on a stick.

blocks.html_en: This particular thread of ice cream was beginning to wear out by the mid-seventies. The products being introduced were popular enough, but they were cheap and mainly bought by kids. Slowly, more people got home freezers, which opened space for bigger, take-home tubs of ice cream and supermarket multipacks of their own-brand lollies. Companies like Unilever had to come up with something bigger and better if they wanted to avoid going the way of Lyons Maid, which is to say, sliding into total irrelevance. When Walls struck gold with the Cornetto in 1976, it was the first of many answers to one simple question that would guide the company’s strategy for the next five decades: ‘How do you sell ice cream to grown-ups?’

blocks.html_en: In the years after 1976, Walls tried to improve and iterate on the Cornetto without much success. The man who finally managed to do it was Kevin Hillman, a product developer who started at Unilever on a scholarship in 1958 and didn’t leave until his retirement in 2001. For most of that time, he worked in ice cream, doing the imaginative acrobatics that you’d expect from Willy Wonka, but with granular attention to detail in the matter of things like emulsification, viscosity and the complex chemistry of milk. He was once head of product development for Unilever’s take-home ice cream – that is, the big tubs and desserts that you don’t eat on the go (in the ice cream world, all products are divided into take-home or impulse, which refers to Cornettos or anything on a stick).

blocks.html_en: By 1980, Hillman was a product development manager at the new Wall’s production plant in Gloucester. One day, when looking through a Good Housekeeping cookbook that he’d bought his wife, he saw a recipe for millefeuille: three sheets of puff pastry, each one with around 729 layers of buttery carbs and air, mortared with two layers of thick vanilla custard or cream. Hillman began to wonder what an ice cream millefeuille would look like. You could extrude drifts of ice cream, but instead of sandwiching them with pastry – which would soften and warp – you could interpolate them with the thinnest leaves of chocolate, he thought. Until the late seventies, take-home ice cream was a support act to impulse, but Hillman’s team had begun to experiment with ice creams that were good enough to work a crowd. Wall’s had already tried out Arctic roll, wrapping a log of vanilla ice cream in a jam-slicked sleeve of sponge cake, and there were also experiments in strawberry- and chocolate-flavoured log desserts, the foundations of a sundae compacted into a 600ml rectangular ice cream block.

blocks.html_en: The earliest prototypes of Hillman’s idea were basic – just the size of a Vesta matchbox, with rigid layers that tasted great but visually fell flat. But Wall’s discovered that if you squeezed a length of steel pipe in a vice until it had an aperture of just a few millimetres, you could extrude very broad, thin sheets of ice cream in an unbroken stream; in time, they also realised that if you increased the output speed, the ice cream would begin to pile up in collapsing sine waves. The engineers worked on adapting the machinery so that the process of plastic extrusion could be used to make something like edible art. In between each of the dozen ice cream layers, they sprayed atomically thin, stracciatella-style layers of chocolate, using an Elizabethan ruff as a visual reference. The result was a dessert the same size as the Motorola 8000X, an early, brick-like mobile phone that debuted that same year. When the team at Wall’s drafted the patent, they described ‘Composite confection products [that] comprise a multiplicity of superimposed extruded thin layers of extrudable e.g. aerated frozen confection, optionally separated by interleaved very thin second confection layers such as couverture thin enough to be at least partly discontinuous.’ But on the streets, they called it Viennetta.

blocks.html_en: If you’re talking to anyone about ice cream’s greatest generation, Hillman’s name will inevitably come up for the Viennetta alone. But if you press him too hard about it, he gets shy. The Viennetta origin story is the kind of thing that is constantly brought up and broken down and misremembered; we like to hear fairy tales about these kinds of foods – the foods that are everywhere but that none of us knows how to make – but they are painstakingly engineered by teams at costs running into millions to game our dopamine systems into buying more. Hillman knows this better than anyone, which is why, when I interviewed him last year and asked about the lightbulb moment, he politely referred me to a corporate history book (Renewing Unilever: Transformation and Tradition) and left it at that.

blocks.html_en: But when I got him on to the real lineage of this ice cream – the myriad corporate, commercial, industrial and trans-European forces that led to the invention of Viennetta – he jumped right in. The spray guns for those ultra-thin layers of chocolate couverture were a trick they took from Cornettos: ‘Exactly the same technology,’ he noted, ‘is used to spray chocolate as is used to spray paint on cars.’ The ice cream, too, was the same as that used in Cornettos – that bright white, sculptable, continental-style ice cream made using vegetable fat, which gives the ice cream its plastic properties, arguably at the expense of taste. Unilever came from the merger of a Dutch margarine company and a British soap business, which means that it was set up nicely for the rise of highly processed vegetable-fat-based ice creams (Dutch colonial links to Indonesia made coconut oil a sure bet.) Then there was the packaging, which was borrowed from Unilever’s German ice cream brand, Langnese.

blocks.html_en: ‘We had very close links. We could pick up the phone and get anything from [other Unilever factories in] Europe,’ Hillman told me. This is how Britain came to host the most productive decade in ice cream, globally, ever: it didn’t do it alone. Unilever had been slowly acquiring ice cream businesses from across the continent for decades. That particular white ice cream is a rethink of an Italian ice cream, perfected under Unilever’s Belgian business, marketed in the UK. Sometimes the impetus for creativity is romance, but most of the time it’s something more prosaic – a Medici, or a Unilever. The story of ice cream is really one of corporate tactics and injections of cash, of the movements of huge companies to create, and then aggressively enforce, a new agenda.

blocks.html_en: After Viennetta blew up, Unilever tried to squeeze a few more ice creams from that basic idea. They developed things like Romantica, Carissima, Sonata and Cassata Denice – all Italianate ice cream gateaux with the kinds of names a person would use to catfish on a sugar daddy site. In 1985, the company started ‘Project Renaissance’, exploring the hypothetical that ice cream could be, instead of a kids’ thing, ‘a secret affair – a lover to be “used”’. Look through the patent records and you’ll find dozens of patents for new ice cream ideas. There’s an ice cream inside a brandysnap-style tuile, capped with waxy chocolate at the ends. There’s another for a lolly made using tiny pellets of fruit ice, poured into a mould, and then frozen together with a contrasting-flavour ice cement. Everyone was doing it. Over at Lyons Maid, they rebranded their choc ice as Figaro and developed the Caprice – a chocolate bar with malt ice cream and caramel that now persists only in lore. Nutcracker, a vanilla ice cream bar with toffee sauce and peanuts, joined Caprice in what was marketed at the time as an ‘adult connoisseur range’.

blocks.html_en: The trouble with marketing ice cream to adults is that novelty isn’t enough. You need things to actually taste great, or at least to taste as luxe as they look. In the eighties, the principles of ice cream began to change, with a new focus on ingredient quality. Lyons Maid introduced a Gold Seal range, then Crème de la Crème – seemingly arbitrary gradations of luxuriousness. In France, Carte d’Or found a path from wholesale into the retail market. Pillsbury bought and popularised the pseudo-Scandinavian Häagen-Dazs. Ben & Jerry’s, which started as a shop in a Vermont garage, opened its first factory in 1985, sold on the strength of its countercultural credentials and natural ingredients. ‘Wanted!’ ran one Lyons Maid advert. ‘Real chocolate, real goodness, real fruit and double cream.’

blocks.html_en: Around this time, European subsidiaries of Unilever were developing a simple ice cream – vanilla, enrobed in chocolate, on a stick. It was the polar opposite of Cornetto and Viennetta, despite working towards the same grown-up principles. It had real vanilla ice cream, enriched not with coconut oil but with butterfat. Whereas most of the chocolate that Unilever had been using was imitation – cheap and adaptable, setting either to a waxy cap or the thinnest layer of craquelure – for this ice cream it developed a better kind of chocolate, one that could be deep-frozen, and that snapped loudly into big, angular shards, but still melted in the mouth. They experimented with the recipe, took it back to basics, and gave the lolly a smooth, cursive silhouette. The industry, which for much of the eighties had evolved in the same implausible way as a deep-sea fish, returned to simple forms. The Magnum debuted in Germany in 1989, and hit the UK the year after.

blocks.html_en: At the end of the day, a Magnum is a choc ice. But what a choc ice! ‘Magnumize your free time’, an ad would say, and show a woman lock the kids outside, so she can go hard on her Magnum in peace. ‘Magnumize your life’: at the office, she has unplugged the landline master socket. (It’s hard to capture just how horny the Magnum was.) If Wall’s started selling ice cream to get through the fallow summer months, then Unilever smashed the final frontier by finding a way to market ice cream all year round – any time, any place. It wasn’t about the sun or refreshment any more, but just an adult’s right to a moment of pleasure. In 1990, for their first big stunt, and the last truly exciting day in British ice cream, Magnums were handed out to thousands of commuters in three major London stations, in rush hour, in November. Within a couple of years, it was the best-selling ice cream in the world, and remains so today.

sentences.zh: 1990 年，他们在 11 月高峰时段向伦敦三个主要车站的数千名通勤者分发了 Magnums，这是他们的第一次大型特技表演，也是英国冰淇淋中最后一次真正令人兴奋的一天。

sentences.en: Within a couple of years, it was the best-selling ice cream in the world, and remains so today.
sentences.zh: 几年之内，它就成为世界上最畅销的冰淇淋，并且至今仍然如此。

blocks.html_en: ‘Of all the fast foods on sale in Britain,’ the food writer Jane Grigson wrote in the Observer at the start of 1990, ‘I would say that vanilla ice cream represents the most catastrophic fall from original virtue.’ But Grigson died just a couple of months later and so I have to wonder if she ever got the chance to try a Magnum?

sentences.en: ‘Of all the fast foods on sale in Britain,’ the food writer Jane Grigson wrote in the Observer at the start of 1990, ‘I would say that vanilla ice cream represents the most catastrophic fall from original virtue.’
sentences.zh: “在英国出售的所有快餐食品中，”美食作家简·格里格森 (Jane Grigson) 1990 年初在《观察家报》上写道，“我想说，香草冰淇淋代表了对原始美德的最灾难性的堕落。”

sentences.en: But Grigson died just a couple of months later and so I have to wonder if she ever got the chance to try a Magnum?
sentences.zh: 但格里格森几个月后就去世了，所以我想知道她是否有机会尝试玛格南？

blocks.html_en: The ice creams that came out of the golden age are as much a part of British food culture as cheddar cheese is. In fact, there are a lot of parallels between the two. Like cheese, ice cream is a dairy product that was given new vitality in the eighties. In the case of cheese, it was by looking back to traditional methods of cheesemaking. In the case of the ice cream, it was innovation, rather than revival, and it happened on the biggest imaginable scale. But unlike the cheese side of the dairy industry, which has continued to thrive, ice cream has stagnated.

sentences.en: The ice creams that came out of the golden age are as much a part of British food culture as cheddar cheese is.
sentences.zh: 黄金时代出现的冰淇淋和切达干酪一样是英国饮食文化的一部分。

sentences.en: In fact, there are a lot of parallels between the two.
sentences.zh: 事实上，两者之间有很多相似之处。

sentences.en: Like cheese, ice cream is a dairy product that was given new vitality in the eighties.
sentences.zh: 与奶酪一样，冰淇淋是八十年代被赋予新活力的乳制品。

sentences.en: In the case of cheese, it was by looking back to traditional methods of cheesemaking.
sentences.zh: 就奶酪而言，这是通过回顾传统的奶酪制作方法来实现的。

sentences.en: In the case of the ice cream, it was innovation, rather than revival, and it happened on the biggest imaginable scale.
sentences.zh: 就冰淇淋而言，这是创新，而不是复兴，而且它的规模是可想象的最大。

sentences.en: But unlike the cheese side of the dairy industry, which has continued to thrive, ice cream has stagnated.
sentences.zh: 但与持续蓬勃发展的乳制品行业的奶酪部分不同，冰淇淋却停滞不前。

blocks.html_en: It’s not like people haven’t tried. In the early nineties, Kevin Hillman was fine-tuning the recipe for a new fruit version of Romantica – a Viennetta-inspired gateau constructed with stacked rosettes of vanilla and strawberry ice cream and sprinkled with beads of fruit ice. He found that if you used a kind of rudimentary shower head, you could spray globular drops of fruit syrup into a bath of liquid nitrogen, where they instantly froze into hailstones. Romantica never took off, but the idea was eventually recycled as Calippo – and then Solero – Shots: tiny pellets of fruit ice that you tipped back like the crumbs at the end of a bag of crisps. This was, for ice cream aficionados, a moment of hope, but these were discontinued within a few years and nothing good has really happened since.

sentences.en: It’s not like people haven’t tried.
sentences.zh: 人们并不是没有尝试过。

sentences.en: In the early nineties, Kevin Hillman was fine-tuning the recipe for a new fruit version of Romantica – a Viennetta-inspired gateau constructed with stacked rosettes of vanilla and strawberry ice cream and sprinkled with beads of fruit ice.
sentences.zh: 九十年代初，凯文·希尔曼 (Kevin Hillman) 正在微调新水果版 Romantica 的配方——这是一种以维也纳塔 (Viennetta) 为灵感的蛋糕，由堆叠的香草和草莓冰淇淋玫瑰花结构成，并撒上果冰珠。

sentences.en: He found that if you used a kind of rudimentary shower head, you could spray globular drops of fruit syrup into a bath of liquid nitrogen, where they instantly froze into hailstones.
sentences.zh: 他发现，如果你使用一种简单的淋浴喷头，你可以将球状的果糖浆喷入液氮浴中，它们会立即冻结成冰雹。

sentences.zh: Romantica 从未流行起来，但这个想法最终被重新利用为 Calippo 和 Solero Shots：小颗粒的果冰，你可以像一袋薯片底部的面包屑一样向后倾斜。

sentences.zh: 对于冰淇淋爱好者来说，这是一个充满希望的时刻，但这些产品在几年内就停产了，从那以后没有什么真正发生过。

blocks.html_en: Today, if you look in that corner-shop freezer cabinet, there will be a Cornetto, a malformed Twister, and then a clade of Magnums: classic, double caramel, white chocolate, almond, mint. The novelties: Starchaser Chocolate Caramel & Popcorn; Gold Caramel Billionaire; Sunlover White Chocolate. Even in the same flavours, Magnums keep on finding culinary synonyms, from vegan Magnums to Magnum ice cream tubs (the chocolate shell turned into an upper crust), mini Magnums and Magnum bites. Everything else, from the chocolate ice cream bars launched by Mars, to the Solero, is a version of a Magnum. It never ends. Last year, Unilever demerged its entire ice cream portfolio, including all the ice creams of the Wall’s Golden Age, and remerged them into a new entity: The Magnum Ice Cream Company. The Magnum has ended up more famous than the company that birthed it.

sentences.zh: 即使口味相同，Magnum 也不断寻找烹饪同义词，从纯素 Magnum 到 Magnum 冰淇淋桶（巧克力壳变成上层外壳）、迷你 Magnum 和 Magnum 咬一口。

blocks.html_en: Last year I went to a food industry expo at London’s ExCel Centre to see if the industry was turning out ice creams that I didn’t yet know about, but should. I hoped to see the prototypes of a new generation of ice creams, the technological and imaginative vanguard. What I saw was a vegan non-Cornetto brand at an unmanned stall. There was a Romanian manufacturer of ice creams modelled after Magnums, making a push for relevance after Unilever entered the Romanian market with the real thing. There were health-food anti-Soleros made from plant juice, fibre and pulp. A Slovenian brand had a product poster that could have been photocopied and transliterated from a Wall’s decal from 1989: Everest was a facsimile of a Magnum, Turbo was a Magic-Ice brand Twister, Free was a Maxibon. The only thing that really spoke to the idiosyncrasies of Slovenian taste was Adore – a mini imitation-Viennetta on a stick. I told Kevin Hillman about it, and he started asking questions that I couldn’t answer about exactly how many layers this thing had.

blocks.html_en: Near the exit of the expo, there was a stall from Jude’s, an upscale British brand in the same vein as Häagen-Dazs. Maybe it’s a sign of how much things have changed that now British ice cream, like cheese, can sell itself on how British it is. They were handing out samples. Clotted cream was doing well. Chocolate, always. The salesperson told me they were doing something different from the multinationals. They tried to give me a sample of ‘blue vanilla’ ice cream coloured with spirulina.

blocks.html_en: Behind, in the freezer cabinet, there were legally daring Jude’s not-Rockets and not-Mini Milks, indistinguishable at a glance from the real thing. The Jude’s version of a Twister was called a Fruit Twist: the same maypole but vegan, smaller, lower sugar. I want to say it’s all outdated, but nothing resonates with the current moment quite like constantly reliving, without resolution or growth, the limited victories of the fifteen years that transformed British ice cream culture. Jude’s biggest line was a range of ice cream sticks, not Magnums, but not not Magnums. They were rounded, slightly fatter at the bottom, with dairy ice cream in a thick chocolate shell. Belgian chocolate, salted caramel, peanut butter – the same as always and, maybe, as good as we’ll ever get.

content_html_zh:
早上好，欢迎来到维特尔斯。 Ruby Tandoh 今天的文章讲述的是英国冰淇淋文化最具影响力的十五年——从 1976 年到 1991 年的繁荣时期，今天英国冰箱里的大多数冰淇淋都是在这段时期发明的。 本文改编自鲁比上个月出版的平装本《All Consuming》一书。 如需购买，请点击此处。

今天的文章也是我们关于影响力的在线系列文章的一部分，该系列文章与上周正式出版的第三期印刷版《影响者》相关。 感谢迄今为止购买副本的所有人！ 您可以在这里订购一份，当您在那里时，您也可以附上一份 Ruby 的冰淇淋指南。

英国冰淇淋的黄金时代始于一个足够简单的策略：必须有一种包装标志性蛋卷冰淇淋的方法。 如果您不必在海边冰淇淋小屋或临时冰淇淋车外排队，而是可以走进一家商店（任何一家商店），找到一个预制的短号，会怎么样？ 如果它被固定得每次都是完美的——这样光滑、浓密的冰淇淋就会一直进入圆锥体，这样酱汁就会流过褶边，永远不会完全冻结，也永远不会滴落？ 如果你能让冰淇淋在物理上不可能从蛋筒上掉下来怎么办？

一家名为 Spica 的意大利制造商已于 1959 年制定了该配方。 成功的部分原因在于 Spica 设计的圆锥体：一种斜切、脆脆的威化饼结构，内部喷洒了巧克力和椰子油的混合物，在威化饼和冰淇淋之间形成了防潮屏障。 但冰淇淋也很重要。 当你尝试用管道输送或像这样储存它时，全乳冰淇淋不能很好地保存。 新的冰淇淋是不同的。 舌头上感觉更冷了。 它融化得很快，但很平稳，就像赛车手干净利落地急转弯一样精确。 你最终得到的是一个由致密充气的植物脂肪乳液制成的短角，上面涂有酱汁，主要作为巧克力塞的借口。

这种冰淇淋在冰淇淋的故乡很受欢迎，但在英国，这个想法并没有立即得到普及。 湿冰淇淋在酥脆的糖筒中只能保存很长时间，然后就会开始分解，而博尔顿一家街角商店的冰淇淋营业额与里米尼一家商店的营业额不同。 因此，当英国冰淇淋界最响亮的品牌 Wall's 试图在 60 年代中期在英国推出这款冰淇淋时，结果失败了。 又花了十年的化学调整才达到了不可能的最佳点：一种具有聚四氟乙烯物理特性的冰淇淋，可以承受在冷冻柜中的碰撞，但也会在嘴里融化。 最终他们成功了，沃尔的母公司联合利华买下了这个配方。 1976 年夏天，Cornetto 进入英国街角商店。

那年夏天，Cornetto 的销量接近 700 万张。 没有比这更好的时间来发布冰淇淋了。 那是有记录以来最热的夏天之一，冰淇淋季节一直延续到秋季，同年，半豪华冰淇淋连锁店 Baskin-Robbins 和 Dayvilles 都进入了英国市场，让人们习惯了这样的想法：你可能要花 25 便士买一个蛋卷冰淇淋。 沃尔斯大力营销，推出了一场病毒式营销活动——歌曲《Just One Cornetto》。 十年之内，Cornetto 推出了草莓、薄荷、朗姆酒和葡萄干等多种口味，年销量达 7000 万份。 这是迄今为止英国生产的最受欢迎的冰淇淋。

在英国冰淇淋界，1976 年是一个具有影响力的十五年紫色时期的开始，它催生了今天冰箱里几乎所有的冰淇淋。 去商店或浏览冰淇淋车侧面的菜单。 你看到迷你牛奶了吗？ 1976. 有趣的脚——小黄人和小猪佩奇形状的去皮雕塑冰淇淋的鼻祖——于 1980 年首次亮相。 Twister，螺旋冰淇淋和果汁冰糕的混合体？ 这种形式于 1982 年在爱尔兰发明，当时是一种草莓、香草和巧克力冰淇淋，具有今天的口味——酸橙、菠萝和草莓三重奏——据称，不可思议的是，这是 1987 年一位女学生在 Jim’ll Fix It 的帮助下参观格洛斯特墙工厂的结果。 Viennetta 发明于 1982 年。 Calippo 于 1982 年进入英国，但橙色 Calippo 直到 1988 年才推出。 盛宴——一种可怕的冰淇淋，看起来像硬壳蟑螂一样无法杀死——是 1983 年的事。 1988 年，我们推出了火星冰淇淋棒。 1990年，荣获金奖。 这一时期的结束是 1990 年推出的另一款冰淇淋巨头，甚至超越了 Cornetto：Magnum——当今世界上最受欢迎的冰淇淋。

冰淇淋文化的突然飞跃可能看起来很神秘，但一旦食品达到工业规模，事情往往就是这样运作的。 变化迅速发生，创新一波又一波地涌来，并因经济变化、兼并、收购和低风险的企业军备竞赛而放大。 20 世纪 30 年代，巧克力也出现了这样的情况，Mars 巧克力棒、士力架、Milky Bar、Maltesers、Aero、Ritter Sport、Rolos 和 KitKats 的发布——这些巧克力棒的正式产品在近一个世纪后我们还没有进行任何有意义的改进。 过去几年也发生了类似的事情：脆味调味料迎来了前所未有的创造力时代。 冰淇淋的黄金时代只有十五年，大致覆盖了七十年代末和八十年代，但它见证了英国工业食品文化在过去半个世纪中最大的爆发。

当冰淇淋于 1800 年代末在英国流行时，很难想象事情会发展到这一步。 意大利移民在街上出售廉价的牛奶冰，摊贩们一大早聚集在运河上购买冰块，然后分散到城市各处。 牛奶与糖一起冷冻，也许还有鸡蛋；用旧抹布擦拭玻璃杯，然后按订单重新装满。 随着时间的推移，冰淇淋变得更加复杂。三十年代，餐饮和咖啡馆帝国里昂制作了冰淇淋蛋糕——像 Trocadero Wonder Gateau 和 Glace Pompadour 这样的夸张蛋糕，冰淇淋的造型就像舞会礼服裙一样。

第二次世界大战开始时，有一队骑着三轮车的男子在销售 Wall’s 品牌的冰淇淋。Wall’s 是一家香肠制造商，他们敏锐地意识到，人们在夏季并不会真正购买猪肉馅饼，因此它可能需要第二个收入来源，该收入来源已于 1922 年被联合利华的前身收购。 然而，冰淇淋与战争无关，而且该行业可以使用的乳制品和糖的数量受到限制。 到了五十年代，冰淇淋比以往任何时候都更加简单。大多数里昂冰淇淋（最终被纳入 Lyons Maid 旗下）都具有严格的功能：砖块、砖块、杯子、柱子和矩形巧克力冰。

随着1954年配给制的结束，战时对食品的最后限制被取消，消费能力增强。 战争期间，冰淇淋三轮车车队被出售和报废，但取而代之的是冰淇淋车和便利店。 Wall’s 曾经 90% 的冰淇淋是在路上销售的，现在 90% 的冰淇淋都是在实体店宽敞的冷冻柜中出售的，他们可以向店主要求独家经营权。 突然之间，几乎是无中生有，有机会做一些新的事情。

按照今天的标准，第一个技术先进的冰淇淋是基本的。 以 Lyons Maid Mivvi 为例，这是一款 1959 年首次推出的棒状香草冰淇淋，配有草莓或橙子冰壳和香草冰淇淋。 它很简单，但以当时一些最复杂的技术为基础。 果味糖浆从塑料动脉泵入一排模具中，这是一种双手操作，模具随着脉冲及时前进。 机械臂在低温盐水浴中摆动模具，动作非常平滑，人眼可以清晰地看到，在此期间，几毫米厚的果冰外壳冻结在金属的轮廓上。 之后，随着弗拉门戈舞者手腕的响动，模具被翻转，将未冷冻的中心倒入一个桶中。 然后，冰淇淋通过精确的金属嘴被输送到空壳中，木制棒棒糖棒从传送带两侧的枪口射出。 像这样的机器每小时可以生产数万个草莓片。 推出后，超过三分之一的 Lyons Maid 冰淇淋都是棒状冰淇淋。

六七十年代的技术变革催生了主要面向儿童的冰淇淋，这在十年前也是不可想象的。 我们买了鬼屋冰棒，白色的牛奶冰上印有蓝色的鬼魂。 一款受德古拉启发的新血红色棒棒糖具有中世纪石像鬼的工匠线条。 当你舔魔法怪物棒棒糖时，弗兰肯斯坦怪物的脸会透过冰块显现出来。 Fab——草莓冰的衬裙，香草冰淇淋的包裹物和撒有珠子的巧克力的外层——的灵感来自《雷鸟》中佩内洛普夫人的 FAB1 劳斯莱斯。

这种特殊的冰淇淋线到了七十年代中期就开始磨损。 推出的产品足够受欢迎，但价格便宜，主要是孩子们买的。 慢慢地，越来越多的人拥有了家用冰柜，这为更大的带回家的冰淇淋桶和超市的自有品牌棒棒糖多包装打开了空间。 像联合利华这样的公司如果想避免重蹈 Lyons Maid 的覆辙，就必须想出更大、更好的产品，也就是说，避免陷入完全无关紧要的境地。 1976 年，当沃尔斯凭借 Cornetto 获得金牌时，它是对一个简单问题的第一个答案，这个问题将指导公司未来 50 年的战略：“如何向成年人出售冰淇淋？”

1976 年之后的几年里，沃尔斯尝试改进和迭代 Cornetto，但没有取得太大成功。 最终成功做到这一点的是凯文·希尔曼 (Kevin Hillman)，他是一名产品开发人员，1958 年凭借奖学金开始在联合利华工作，直到 2001 年退休才离开。 在那段时间里，他大部分时间都在冰淇淋行业工作，做着威利·旺卡（Willy Wonka）所期待的富有想象力的杂技，但他对乳化、粘度和牛奶复杂化学等问题的细节非常关注。 他曾经是联合利华带回家冰淇淋的产品开发主管，即你不在旅途中吃的大桶冰淇淋和甜点（在冰淇淋世界中，所有产品都分为带回家或冲动，指的是Cornettos或任何棒状冰淇淋）。

1980 年，Hillman 成为 Wall 位于格洛斯特的新生产工厂的产品开发经理。 有一天，当他翻阅给妻子买的一本《好管家》食谱时，他看到了一份千层酥的食谱：三片酥皮，每片含有约 729 层黄油碳水化合物和空气，并用两层厚厚的香草蛋奶冻或奶油涂抹。 希尔曼开始思考冰淇淋千层酥会是什么样子。 他认为，你可以挤出大量的冰淇淋，但你可以在其中插入最薄的巧克力叶，而不是用糕点将它们夹在中间——糕点会软化和变形。 直到七十年代末，带回家的冰淇淋还是一种冲动的支持行为，但希尔曼的团队已经开始尝试适合人群的冰淇淋。 Wall’s 已经尝试过北极卷，将一根香草冰淇淋包裹在光滑的果酱海绵蛋糕套中，还尝试了草莓和巧克力口味的原木甜点，将圣代的基础压缩成 600 毫升的矩形冰淇淋块。

希尔曼想法的最早原型是基本的——只有维斯塔火柴盒大小，有刚性的层，味道很好，但视觉上很平淡。 但沃尔发现，如果你用虎钳挤压一段钢管，直到它的孔径只有几毫米，你就可以不间断地挤出非常宽、薄的冰淇淋片；随着时间的推移，他们还意识到，如果提高输出速度，冰淇淋就会开始以折叠的正弦波堆积起来。 工程师们致力于改造机器，以便塑料挤压过程可以用来制作类似食用艺术品的东西。 在十几个冰淇淋层之间，他们使用伊丽莎白时代的领子作为视觉参考，喷涂了原子薄的斯特拉恰特拉式巧克力层。 结果是一款与摩托罗拉 8000X 大小相同的甜点，摩托罗拉 8000X 是一款早期的砖块状手机，于同年推出。 当 Wall's 的团队起草专利时，他们描述了“复合糖果产品”，其中包含多个叠加的可挤出薄层，例如糖果。充气冷冻甜食，可选地由交错的非常薄的第二甜食层分隔，例如足够薄以至少部分不连续的糖皮。 但在街上，他们称之为Viennetta。

如果你和任何人谈论冰淇淋最伟大的一代，希尔曼的名字将不可避免地只出现在维也纳。 但如果你在这件事上逼迫他太多，他就会变得害羞。 Viennetta 的起源故事是一种不断被提起、分解和错误记忆的事情。我们喜欢听关于这类食物的童话故事——这些食物无处不在，但我们没人知道如何制作——但它们是由团队花费数百万美元精心设计的，目的是博弈我们的多巴胺系统，让我们购买更多食物。 希尔曼比任何人都更了解这一点，这就是为什么当我去年采访他并询问灵光一现的时刻时，他礼貌地向我推荐了一本企业历史书（更新联合利华：转型与传统），然后就不再阅读了。

但当我让他了解这种冰淇淋的真正血统时——无数的企业、商业、工业和跨欧洲的力量导致了 Viennetta 的发明——他立即跳了起来。 用于超薄巧克力层的喷枪是他们从 Cornettos 那里学来的技巧：“与在汽车上喷漆所用的技术完全相同，”他指出，“用于喷涂巧克力。” 冰淇淋也与Cornettos中使用的冰淇淋相同——这种亮白色、可塑形的欧陆式冰淇淋是用植物脂肪制成的，这赋予了冰淇淋可塑性，但可以说是以牺牲味道为代价的。 联合利华是由一家荷兰人造黄油公司和一家英国肥皂公司合并而成的，这意味着它的成立非常适合高度加工的植物脂肪冰淇淋的兴起（荷兰殖民时期与印度尼西亚的联系使得椰子油成为必然的选择。） 然后是包装，借鉴了联合利华旗下的德国冰淇淋品牌Langnese。

“我们有着非常密切的联系。 我们可以拿起电话从欧洲（联合利华的其他工厂）获取任何东西，”希尔曼告诉我。 这就是英国如何在全球范围内迎来有史以来冰淇淋产量最高的十年：它并不是独自做到的。 几十年来，联合利华一直在慢慢收购整个非洲大陆的冰淇淋业务。 这种特殊的白色冰淇淋是对意大利冰淇淋的重新思考，在联合利华的比利时业务下完善，在英国销售。 有时创造力的动力是浪漫，但大多数时候它是更平淡的东西——美第奇或联合利华。 冰淇淋的故事实际上是企业策略和现金注入的故事，是大公司创建并积极执行新议程的行动。

Viennetta 爆炸后，联合利华试图从这一基本理念中挤出更多冰淇淋。 他们开发了 Romantica、Carissima、Sonata 和 Cassata Denice 等产品，这些都是意大利冰淇淋蛋糕，名字就像人们在糖爹网站上钓鱼时用的名字一样。 1985 年，该公司启动了“文艺复兴计划”，探索这样一个假设：冰淇淋可能不再是孩子们的玩意，而是“一种秘密的事物——一种被“利用”的情人”。 翻阅专利记录，您会发现数十项新冰淇淋创意的专利。 白兰地风格的薄纱里有一个冰淇淋，末端覆盖着蜡质巧克力。 另一种是用小粒果冰制成的棒棒糖，倒入模具中，然后与对比口味的冰水泥一起冷冻。 每个人都在这样做。 在 Lyons Maid，他们将巧克力冰重新命名为 Figaro，并开发了 Caprice——一种含有麦芽冰淇淋和焦糖的巧克力棒，现在只存在于传说中。 胡桃夹子是一款配有太妃糖酱和花生的香草冰淇淋，加入了 Caprice 的行列，当时的营销定位是“成人鉴赏家系列”。

向成年人推销冰淇淋的问题在于新奇还不够。 你需要东西真正尝起来很棒，或者至少尝起来像它们看起来一样奢华。 八十年代，冰淇淋的原理开始发生变化，新的重点是成分质量。 Lyons Maid 推出了 Gold Seal 系列，然后推出了 Crème de la Crème - 看似随意的奢华层次。 在法国，Carte d’Or找到了一条从批发市场进入零售市场的道路。 皮尔斯伯里购买并推广了伪斯堪的纳维亚哈根达斯。 Ben & Jerry's 最初是佛蒙特州车库里的一家商店，于 1985 年开设了第一家工厂，凭借其反文化背景和天然成分进行销售。 '通缉！' 刊登了一则里昂女仆广告。 “真正的巧克力、真正的美味、真正的水果和双层奶油。”

大约在这个时候，联合利华的欧洲子公司正在开发一种简单的冰淇淋——香草冰淇淋，外面裹着巧克力，放在棍子上。 尽管他们努力遵循相同的成人原则，但它与科尔内托和维内塔截然相反。 它有真正的香草冰淇淋，不是用椰子油而是用乳脂。 联合利华一直使用的大部分巧克力都是仿制品——价格便宜、适应性强，要么装在蜡质的盖子上，要么装在最薄的裂纹层上——而联合利华却为这款冰淇淋开发了一种更好的巧克力，一种可以深度冷冻的巧克力，可以大声地折断成大而有棱角的碎片，但在嘴里仍然融化。 他们尝试了配方，回归基础，赋予棒棒糖光滑的草书轮廓。 在八十年代的大部分时间里，这个行业都以与深海鱼类同样令人难以置信的方式发展，现在又回到了简单的形式。 Magnum 于 1989 年在德国首次亮相，并于次年登陆英国。

归根结底，Magnum 就是一块巧克力冰。 但多么巧克力的冰啊！ 一则广告会说，“充分利用你的空闲时间”，并展示一位女士将孩子锁在外面，这样她就可以安心地使用她的 Magnum。 “丰富你的生活”：在办公室，她拔掉了固定电话总插座。 （很难描述 Magnum 到底有多饥渴。） 如果说沃尔开始销售冰淇淋是为了度过夏季的闲暇时光，那么联合利华则通过找到一种全年、任何时间、任何地点销售冰淇淋的方式，打破了最后的前沿。 这不再是阳光或茶点的问题，而是成年人享受片刻快乐的权利。 1990 年，他们在 11 月高峰时段向伦敦三个主要车站的数千名通勤者分发了 Magnums，这是他们的第一次大型特技表演，也是英国冰淇淋中最后一次真正令人兴奋的一天。 几年之内，它就成为世界上最畅销的冰淇淋，并且至今仍然如此。

“在英国出售的所有快餐食品中，”美食作家简·格里格森 (Jane Grigson) 1990 年初在《观察家报》上写道，“我想说，香草冰淇淋代表了对原始美德的最灾难性的堕落。” 但格里格森几个月后就去世了，所以我想知道她是否有机会尝试玛格南？

黄金时代出现的冰淇淋和切达干酪一样是英国饮食文化的一部分。 事实上，两者之间有很多相似之处。 与奶酪一样，冰淇淋是八十年代被赋予新活力的乳制品。 就奶酪而言，这是通过回顾传统的奶酪制作方法来实现的。 就冰淇淋而言，这是创新，而不是复兴，而且它的规模是可想象的最大。 但与持续蓬勃发展的乳制品行业的奶酪部分不同，冰淇淋却停滞不前。

人们并不是没有尝试过。 九十年代初，凯文·希尔曼 (Kevin Hillman) 正在微调新水果版 Romantica 的配方——这是一种以维也纳塔 (Viennetta) 为灵感的蛋糕，由堆叠的香草和草莓冰淇淋玫瑰花结构成，并撒上果冰珠。 他发现，如果你使用一种简单的淋浴喷头，你可以将球状的果糖浆喷入液氮浴中，它们会立即冻结成冰雹。 Romantica 从未流行起来，但这个想法最终被重新利用为 Calippo 和 Solero Shots：小颗粒的果冰，你可以像一袋薯片底部的面包屑一样向后倾斜。 对于冰淇淋爱好者来说，这是一个充满希望的时刻，但这些产品在几年内就停产了，从那以后没有什么真正发生过。

今天，如果你看看街角商店的冷冻柜，你会发现有一种 Cornetto、一种畸形的 Twister，然后是 Magnum 的一个分支：经典、双焦糖、白巧克力、杏仁、薄荷。 新奇产品：追星巧克力焦糖和爆米花；金焦糖亿万富翁；太阳恋人白巧克力。 即使口味相同，Magnum 也不断寻找烹饪同义词，从纯素 Magnum 到 Magnum 冰淇淋桶（巧克力壳变成上层外壳）、迷你 Magnum 和 Magnum 咬一口。 其他一切，从玛氏推出的巧克力冰淇淋棒，到 Solero，都是 Magnum 的一个版本。 它永远不会结束。 去年，联合利华拆分了其整个冰淇淋产品组合，包括长城黄金时代的所有冰淇淋，并将它们重新合并为一个新实体：玛格南冰淇淋公司。 Magnum 最终比它的诞生公司更有名。

去年，我去了伦敦 ExCel 中心举行的食品工业博览会，看看该行业是否正在生产我还不知道但应该知道的冰淇淋。 我希望看到新一代冰淇淋的原型，即技术和想象力的先锋。 我看到的是一个无人摊位上的纯素非Cornetto品牌。 罗马尼亚一家冰淇淋制造商效仿 Magnums，在联合利华以真品进入罗马尼亚市场后，力图提升相关性。 还有由植物汁、纤维和果肉制成的保健食品抗索莱罗斯。 斯洛文尼亚的一个品牌有一张产品海报，可以从 1989 年的 Wall 贴花上复印和音译：Everest 是 Magnum 的复制品，Turbo 是 Magic-Ice 品牌的 Twister，Free 是 Maxibon。 唯一能真正体现斯洛文尼亚品味特质的是 Adore——一种迷你仿制维埃内塔（Viennetta）。 我告诉凯文·希尔曼（Kevin Hillman）这件事，他开始问我无法回答的问题，即这个东西到底有多少层。

在世博会出口附近，有一个与哈根达斯同类型的英国高档品牌Jude's的摊位。 也许这表明事情已经发生了很大的变化，现在英国冰淇淋就像奶酪一样，可以以其英国特色来推销自己。 他们正在分发样品。 凝结奶油表现良好。 巧克力，永远。 销售人员告诉我，他们正在做一些与跨国公司不同的事情。 他们试图给我一份用螺旋藻着色的“蓝色香草”冰淇淋样品。

后面的冷冻柜里，放着合法大胆的裘德的非火箭队和非迷你牛奶，乍一看与真品没有什么区别。 Jude 版本的 Twister 被称为 Fruit Twist：同样的五月花柱，但纯素，更小，含糖量更低。 我想说这一切都已经过时了，但没有什么比不断重温十五年来改变英国冰淇淋文化的有限胜利更能与当前时刻产生共鸣的了，没有决心或成长。 裘德最大的产品系列是一系列冰淇淋棒，不是万能冰淇淋，但也不是万能冰淇淋。 它们是圆形的，底部稍胖，厚厚的巧克力壳里有乳制品冰淇淋。 比利时巧克力、咸焦糖、花生酱——一如既往，也许是我们能吃到的最好的东西。
